items.title: Prompts Don't Protect: Architectural Enforcement via MCP Proxy for LLM Tool Access Control
items.one_liner: Relying on prompts for LLM tool access control is fundamentally broken, necessitating structural enforcement like an MCP proxy layer.
items.summary: Researchers demonstrate that prompt-based instructions fail to reliably prevent autonomous LLM agents from invoking unauthorized tools, with models selecting them in 48-68% of adversarial scenarios and up to 96% during role escalation attacks. Even explicit per-tool allowlists fail to reduce violations to zero, yielding unauthorized invocation rates between 4.0% and 37.0%. To achieve structural security, the authors propose a proxy-enforced attribute-based access control layer for the Model Context Protocol that filters tool registries at discovery time. By preventing unauthorized tools from ever reaching the model context, this architectural approach guarantees a 0% unauthorized invocation rate.

items.bottom_line: Prompt instructions cannot secure LLM tool access against role escalation or adversarial selection, requiring proxy-enforced architectural controls instead.

items.title: Layered LLM Defenses as an Ensemble: Access Tiers, Inference Cost, and the Measured Failure Correlation Between Defense Layers
items.one_liner: Stacked LLM defense layers exhibit architectural failure correlation, meaning ensemble security must be measured end-to-end rather than assumed.
items.summary: Researchers evaluated stacked LLM defense layers as an ensemble, noting that compounding security relies on members failing on independent inputs. Using the Adversary Access-Tier Model and an inference-cost classification, the study measured failure correlation across a seven-layer stack against an adaptive adversary. The findings show positive failure correlation in all fifteen measurable pairs with phi coefficients ranging from 0.30 to 0.75, driven predominantly by common-cause dependence on the wrapped model. Consequently, the seven-layer stack rejected 80 percent of benign prompts while remaining statistically indistinguishable from its single strongest layer.
items.bottom_line: Layered LLM defenses do not compound independently due to architectural common-cause correlation, leading to high false refusal rates without proportional security gains.

items.title: Recognition Without Enforcement: Configuration-Dependent Failures in LLM Agent Instruction Arbitration and External Control
items.one_liner: LLM agents suffer from a recognition-enforcement gap that allows instruction spoofing, requiring external reference monitors for reliable tool security.
items.summary: Research into LLM agent instruction arbitration reveals a recognition-enforcement gap where models can successfully identify authority spoofing or conflicting tool calls in their activations, yet still execute unauthorized instructions depending on configuration. items.title: When Verified Source Becomes Attack Input: Defending Smart Contracts Against LLM-Based Vulnerability Scanning
items.one_liner: DeLLMGuard is a smart contract deployment framework that thwarts automated LLM vulnerability scanning by separating source code from runtime execution.
items.summary: While publishing and verifying smart contract source code on blockchain explorers builds user trust, it also enables malicious actors and automated LLM agents to scan contracts for vulnerabilities at scale. DeLLMGuard separates disclosed source code from runtime execution across multiple addresses, requiring LLM agents to accurately recover complex proxy, delegate, and factory relationships. items.title: KidnapRAG: A Black-Box Attack for Hijacking Reasoning in Agentic Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
